newsitem.title: USA: U.S. could still get "fast track" in 1997 - Daley.
newsitem.headline: U.S. could still get "fast track" in 1997 - Daley.

text.p: The United States could still approve "fast track" trade legislation this year, Commerce Secretary William Daley said on Tuesday.
Daley, who is in Santiago at the end of a 10-day mission to Brazil, Argentina and Chile, said that the Clinton administration was still trying to determine the right timing to tackle fast track.
"We do have time," Daley said in a teleconference with reporters in Washington. "But more important than getting it introduced is getting it passed."
The U.S. government is currently dealing with a number of weighty issues such as the federal budget deal and the renewal of "most favored nation" trade status for China, Daley said.
But successful outcomes in those cases would strengthen not only Clinton's hand but a bipartisan coalition the White House hopes to put together to pass fast track in Congress, Daley added.
"There's an urgency to lots of things, but there also has to be a timing for everything in life, and what we're trying to determine now is the proper timing to move on it," he said.
Clinton needs fast track authority to expand the North America Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) and add Chile as a partner in the pact, which already includes Canada and Mexico.

However, Daley said that the United States could also strike a bilateral trade deal with Chile as an alternative to expanding NAFTA, which has been under fire from liberal Democrats and conservative Republicans in Congress.
The United States will also need fast track to negotiate from a stronger position with other Latin American countries to establish a Free Trade Agreement of the Americas (FTAA) by the year 2005.
Whichever way, Clinton must have fast track to negotiate with Chile, which has said it will not sit down with the United States unless it secures that authority.
Trade agreements signed under fast track cannot be amended by Congress, which must vote them up or down.
The Clinton administration tried to win fast track authority in 1994 but its efforts foundered in the wake of the Mexican peso crisis in 1995.
Republicans and Democrats also must resolve their differences over what negotiating authority Congress will cede to the president.
Republican congressional leaders have said they will not approve a bill granting Clinton powers to negotiate labor and environmental issues that are not directly linked to trade.

Organized labor and environmental groups have been key Democratic constituencies, but Daley suggested on Monday in Santiago that the White House may soften its insistence those provisions for fast track.
In his Tuesday teleconference, Daley pointed out that the United States was losing business deals while other countries scrambled to make trade agreements.
Chile, for instance, went ahead and signed pacts with Canada, Mexico and the Mercosur, a common market project that includes Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay.
Under those agreements, he said, even U.S. firms like McDonalds or Southwest Bell are importing equipment from Mexico and Canada for their investments in Chle.
Daley said deals like those might put pressure not only on politicians in Washington but in other U.S. interest groups to support trade.

"I would hope it'd make some people aware that there is progress being made by other countries to give opportunities to their companies (and) that will therefore make U.S. companies less competitive," he said.
Daley, who took office in January, said after his first trade mission that he planned to make annual trips to Latin America because he saw so much potential for U.S. businesses in that region.
((Peter Bate, Washington newsroom + 202 898-8306))
